context: A group of 20 learners each count the number of stones they have. The 20 counts are grouped into four equal-width, non-overlapping ranges to draw a histogram.

params.name: f1
params.let: len([v for v in data if v >= l1 and v <= h1])

params.name: f2
params.let: len([v for v in data if v >= l2 and v <= h2])

params.name: f3
params.let: len([v for v in data if v >= l3 and v <= h3])

params.name: f4
params.let: len([v for v in data if v >= l4 and v <= h4])

params.require: f1 >= 1 and f2 >= 1 and f3 >= 1 and f4 >= 1
params.why: every range must hold at least one learner, so that each range really is a bar of the histogram
exactly one tallest bar and exactly one shortest bar, so the words 'the tallest bar' and 'the shortest bar' name a single bar
keep the histogram reasonably even, as a class's data would be

stem: A group of $20$ learners count the number of stones they each have. This is the data they collect: $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{ccccc} {=d1}&{=d2}&{=d3}&{=d4}&{=d5} \\ {=d6}&{=d7}&{=d8}&{=d9}&{=d10} \\ {=d11}&{=d12}&{=d13}&{=d14}&{=d15} \\ {=d16}&{=d17}&{=d18}&{=d19}&{=d20} \end{array}\end{aligned}$ Group the data into these four ranges and draw a histogram: ${=l1}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h1}$, ${=l2}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h2}$, ${=l3}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h3}$ and ${=l4}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h4}$. How many more learners are in the tallest bar of the histogram than in the shortest bar?
solution: Firstly, sort the data from the smallest value to the largest.

Secondly, count how many of the sorted values fall in each range. A value on the edge of a range belongs to that range, because the signs are $\le$. Each count is the height of one bar of the histogram.

${=l1}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h1}$: {=f1} learners; ${=l2}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h2}$: {=f2} learners; ${=l3}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h3}$: {=f3} learners; ${=l4}\le\text{number of stones}\le {=h4}$: {=f4} learners.
Check: ${=f1}+{=f2}+{=f3}+{=f4}=20$, so every learner is counted in exactly one bar.
The tallest bar is {=mx} learners high and the shortest bar is {=mn} learners high.
${=mx}-{=mn}={=mx - mn}$, so the tallest bar has {=mx - mn} more learners than the shortest bar.
notes: Advanced tier: the book's standard items (ex10-3-3/4, ex10-7-12/13) ask for ONE range of an unsorted 4x5 grid of 20 counts. Here the learner must group ALL 20 values into four given equal-width ranges (the book's inclusive form a <= number <= b), i.e. build the whole grouped frequency table, then compare the tallest and shortest bars: several steps, same method (sort, group, read the bar heights). Instances vary: start s in {0,1} and width w in {4,5} give ranges 0-3..12-15, 1-4..13-16, 0-4..15-19 or 1-5..16-20; the 20 data values are drawn independently and uniformly inside the four ranges, so repeats and edge values (e.g. 5, 6, 10, 11) are common, as in the book. Requires: every bar non-empty, a unique tallest and a unique shortest bar (so the wording names one bar each), and a gap of at most 8. The answer is the integer difference of the two heights, never a decimal. Counts were checked in a separate simulation against an independent bucketing (v - s) // w; the four counts always sum to 20. No distractors (numeric). The catalogued mc:g10m10s3-1-1:boundary-value-in-wrong-range is the likely wrong-answer source (an edge value placed in the neighbouring bar) but cannot be tagged on a typed numeric answer; the solution's step 3 states the edge rule explicitly.
